claims.text: A layered architecture enhances the time-dependent plastic-deformation resistance of high-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings.
Chemically and mechanically distinct interfaces act as barriers to diffusion-assisted dislocation climb.
The proposed coating contains layers differing in composition and/or phase, thereby creating distinct interfacial boundaries.
A controlled comparison should subject a multilayer coating and a homogeneous coating of the same overall composition to identical elevated-temperature tensile-creep tests.
High-entropy alloys can undergo lattice-diffusion-controlled, stress-assisted dislocation-climb creep at 500–600 °C.
The relevant comparison should use stresses within a creep regime dominated by lattice-diffusion-mediated dislocation climb.
Layer interfaces varying in composition and mechanical modulus interrupt dislocation motion.
A series of multilayer interfaces blocks or slows dislocation climb and other dislocation motion.
Requiring dislocations to overcome an additional barrier at each interface increases the effective activation energy for creep.
Interface-induced impediment of dislocation motion reduces the overall plastic strain rate.
Under identical creep conditions, the multilayer coating will have a lower steady-state creep rate than the homogeneous coating.
Under identical creep conditions, the multilayer coating will have a higher apparent creep activation energy than the homogeneous coating.
The baseline is a homogeneous high-entropy-alloy coating with the same bulk composition but without engineered multilayer interfaces.
The hypothesis is limited to conditions in which diffusion-controlled dislocation climb dominates, proposed as intermediate temperatures up to about 600 °C and sub-yield stresses.
The multilayer benefit may diminish when mechanisms such as grain-boundary sliding or melting dominate at higher temperatures or stresses.
Interfacial barriers are known to impede dislocation motion in similar material systems.
The quantitative effect of multilayer interfaces on creep activation energy and creep rate remains undetermined.
Failure to obtain a reproducibly lower creep rate or higher activation energy, together with absence of interface-mediated dislocation blocking, would falsify the hypothesis.
